Emily Stoner, the owner of Delmarville's six-week-old gourmet food shop Sabines, was at the next table over from Tyler, the booths running parallel like competing train tracks. Tyler and her father, Dr. Mark Nguyen, were shelling the roasted peanuts they'd won for coming in second, which Tyler had done three years in a row. She passed a handful to Emily, who was still picking at an unpeeled Satsuma tangerine from Tyler's fruit basket.

"How did you think it was going?" Emily asked her.

"I'm pretty sure second is the highest you can place and still win something," Tyler said. "They're just giving me a ruby instead of a gyuto."

"Why do you still enter if it's hopeless?"

"I definitely come to the party with the half-price dessert coupons," Tyler said. But really she had two serious reasons. Winning second meant Dr. Nguyen bought pizza for everybody. And winning second five times in a row now meant the market would stock Tyler's Hot Nuts, which were better than anything else in Delmarville. She was making two hundred dollars a month for three hours' worth of work, and so the Nut Lab as it was called—a chrome mixer, a stack of grocery store trays, and a box of plastic cones by the front window of the house—was just one of many products in the pipe dream assembly line that was her future.

"Are you going to start carrying fruit pies now?" she said. "Because then we'd be competitors."

"No," Emily said, biting a haphazard piece off the edge of the tangerine. She and Mark had dated in college. Despite everything, he still reminded her a little of him. "I thought Daufuskie peach might be nice in January. But by the time it can be stored, I think enough people's New Year's resolutions will have fallen through that January is a lost cause." Tyler laughed. "If anyone was going to bake a pie for the fair, it would've been Audrey Walke. Audrey was the one who cared about things like that."

Tyler winced. Emily was known at Sabines for her personalized recommendations of artisanal foods, but her refrain on Audrey was that she didn't carry anything that woman would want to eat.

"If you put the Walke products in one aisle," Tyler said, "Sabines would be half the size, right?"

Emily waved a tangerine wedge. "I know, I know. I'm sorry.

Tyler started to smile, but stopped himself and stared at the metal table. Margaret raised the ribbon and Tyler glanced up at her. "Present the award," Margaret said. "Son. Pie on, pie off."

Tyler handed the apple pie to the milling children and whispered to Margaret, "She's watching me."

"Who's watching you?"

"Wait until you see my mom."

Tyler took Magnus Eglon by the hand and led him out of the tent. Magnus had a bit of the dribble about him where he let his chin drop.

"Do you know how long I've known you, Tyler," Margaret said, "and every contest, you ask me to tell you how your mom is doing and I tell you the truth."

Tyler and Magnus walked home.

"This pie is too sweet," Victor said, spitting it into the sink. He ate the last dollar of his first pie at five that morning, so he hadn't eaten anything since.

The cherry pie separated like an egg on his fork. Each bite went back into his mouth the same way. One. Back one. Two. Two. One. Two. Two. He remembered tulips, yellow and pink spring tulips, and the roads back from BC when Baker would drive. What was that singer, what was her name? Rita. Rita was her name. She would roll the window down and smoke. There would be a face behind her. One. Back one. A face behind her on the road. The dog would stand up on the back of the car on the seat and then he'd roll down his side. Rita would grab him by the collar and pull him down. Back two. Back one.

He remembered these things and his stomach hurt as if he hadn't eaten in years.

His wife moved out when they lost their market. She used to get up and make him breakfast. There was a face behind her on the road. Victor couldn't tell Margaret he missed a sleeping woman every morning, or the towels she would buy with bees embroidered in the corners, or the things she left in piles on the floor. He ate his fifth piece of pie by mistake, then his sixth.

Evelyn grinned over at Tyler. Even though he'd lost, she figured he must be glad too, because it was no fun waiting all that time to find out.

Margaret cleared her throat. "This year's first-place winner, Tyler, and our mystery baker, for sharing the best pies I've tasted at this fair in years, thank you." Without looking at Evelyn, she said, "I'm sorry about your loss." Then Margaret leaned forward and pinned the blue ribbon above Evelyn's heart.

"Ding dong!" a voice called from the back of the tent as the next pie was set down to cool. "Now you don't have to pretend you don't care anymore!"

Tyler's grandfather, Sonny Tan, strode up to them. "I thought you could use a better postmortem pie, Evelyn. The secret ingredient you want is shortening. It's just the combination of the cherries and the lard that worked out so well."

Margaret's mouth fell open. "Lard? You used lard?" 

He smiled. "Just in a pinch. The recipe had called for butter, but we were fresh out. Any luck down at the market?"

Evelyn stared at Sonny's cherries and thought about how she pictured Sonny in her mind when she recalled the summer of 1985, her first year at county fair. She'd never looked at him like that, up close. He really hadn't changed at all--still wore that silly Hawaiian shirt under a hot robe.

"Don't feel bad," Margaret told them. "I plan to increase the prize money and bake-off dinners next year. My compliments to the mystery baker, if you ever find out who it was."

And she sauntered away.

Tyler laughed. "I guess we both just lost."

Evelyn said, "Congratulations, Tyler, on taking second prize. I haven't made a good pie since your mother was a little girl. I really should be the one handing you a consolation prize. But let's forget about time. You ever hear about joining the CIA when you can't open a car door without bending a fastener? I think I should go find something else to do with the rest of my life. Ready to go get a beer, Tyler?"

That night she couldn't sleep. At 5:45 she was in the kitchen, making a list of the ingredients for a butterscotch pie. Downstairs, the house smelled like mourning.

The following Saturdays, while the rest of the town celebrated summer and the Mabeline B. Swett Memorial Carnival, Evelyn would go to the library and stand in front of the Oregon Cooking Cherry Pies collection. She had known she'd marry Walt the first time she saw the cherry pie recipe with his name next to it. It didn't matter that the recipe belonged to Eleanor Chancellor.She had known it would belong to them.

Cherry pie only interested Evelyn when it became competition. She liked choosing a category—the best of some subset of cooks, the half-pint coconut cream pie or the mixed berry whose exact composition could be argued over. She liked sneaking into the next room to see the contenders' expressions when their names were called. She liked scowling, or rolling her eyes, when a new contest was announced and the question of who would win moved from the center of conversation to its edge.

The letters took longer to write than the pies, and the words not chosen went back into the box.

"Walt buys everything here," she would write to Eleanor. "But he will never get my recipe."

Evelyn's favorite pie was a madras apple pie flavored with crushed chiles and cooked down to a thick, unctuous filling. On weekdays she made it for lunch, and on Sundays she sometimes made it for dinner and brought a tiny piece to her upstairs neighbor, Ruby Clute, who didn't have a husband and couldn't bake, and didn't understand why Evelyn hadn't stopped by more after Walt died.

The Ortizes' house was down the road, sixty novel pages from Evelyn's.

Of course, Evelyn knew how to bake a cherry pie. Pies were her specialty. When she was growing up, she and her mother, Roberta, spent summer evenings and whole Saturdays in the kitchen making rhubarb pies from Roberta's great-grandma's recipe. Roberta taught her how to wait until the berries or cherries or rhubarb softened a bit inside the crust. How to use an ice water bath to get a flaky texture. The trick with sour fruit was to balance it with sugar and sweet spices. If you baked too long or didn't let the steam out of the crust, it could get soggy. And if you didn't use bottled cherry juice instead of emptying the jar, the fruit would end up too sweet.

But Evelyn was always more intent on watching her mother the way some people watch chefs on television. Roberta liked to joke that she was a stay-at-home mom, but most days--fair days included--she was gone from sunrise to sunset at the Metropole in Harlow. Evelyn would sit at the kitchen island in their split level in Marengo as her mother and a few line servers or waitstaff from the restaurant talked business over pie crust. She took great care in mixing the fresh batter, rolling out the circles to fit the pie tins, and lining the edges with crinkled, pleated rows.

Few people actually try to make an edible pie from scratch, which is one reason Evelyn won the contest year after year. Competition aside, she wasn't sure if she knew how to do anything else. After a while, two people came from the direction of the truck. One was a young woman in dirty blue jeans and a long black shirt. The other was an old man in overalls and a flannel shirt. They stood on either side of the young man while he explained something, and every so often he nodded and looked up at the sky. His face was even, serious, proud.

She couldn't see any familiar things about him, though the woman's dark hair was long and curly. When they turned toward the fairgrounds, the sun glinted off something or other that the old man was carrying over his shoulder, and Evelyn felt a moment of joy for them all. But then the woman patted the young man's thigh, and Evelyn understood.

After a moment she bent down, filled her glass jar with thick green milkweed sap, and cradled it in her lap. When the last dot of sap grew across the glass, she carefully dried the outside with her towel and twisted the lid on tight. Tyler had spent weeks worrying about how to hide a pie at registration. He didn't bake very well. Eventually it had seemed easier to just go to the bakery and buy two pies. He'd made his own crusts and brought a box of Twinkies to mix with the filling. Both pies would taste the same. His chances would be even. Once he had a pie, he worried whether the bottom would burn. His mom worked the night shift at Target. He told her not to wake him up, that if he overslept he'd miss the ferry in the morning. What he was really afraid of was that she'd come get him and they'd have to talk.

Tyler went on YouTube and searched classic movie scenes. He found the wedding in The Philadelphia Story. Rex Kramer and George Zucco stood next to each other at a white tablecloth-covered banquet table. Stacks of empty plates sat in front of them. Zucco had a drink in his hand, his arm resting on the tablecloth. Kramer spoke about getting shore leave in Tasmania. Stood on a hill-maybe this was Tasmania-and looked down at the ocean below. He was a military man in a well-tailored uniform. He'd been on a ship for months, maybe years.

Tyler's mom was just as funny in Dark Horse Alley. He turned back to his screen and kept searching. This movie, this one-how about this one? He looked for movie scenes like a kid looking for his favorite toy in its usual hiding place and wondering when he'd lost it last. Some funny, uninteresting scenes, and a few clips from the first two movies that still made him want to laugh. "I know you're there, Ivan, so just get out here!" Kramer said. The camera panned up. Ivan, the sheepdog from the first three movies, stood smiling on top of the hay bales behind Kramer.

A search like this could take months, and the longer it went on, the less likely you were to find what you were looking for. Tyler's mom was in the office, and when she got mad at the printer she lowered her voice and stormed past the vestibule. Tyler had almost quit, but then he'd remembered Last Year at Marienbad. Book Review

Fever Dream

by Samanta Schweblin

Samanta Schweblin finds inspiration in her Argentinian heritage and European explorations in her UNESCO-listed novel, Fever Dream, which is a hybrid tale of myth, mystical realism, history and environmentalism. Narrated by the protagonist via a series of diary entries, this uneasy story draws on Schweblin's extensive interest in biology, art, and the surrounding environment. 

From the beginning of the first entry, we're transported to the mind of the speaker, overlapping and skipping across time as they describe a blistering and brutal heatwave that has overtaken the world. One of the many surreal elements here is the omnipresence of pears; whether due to the heat or a prior quarantine, a number of certain species have died. As this childlike voice grows lax, some evasive elements are uncovered about the possibly sentient phenomena in the area. Human-animal hybrids known as "devolutions" roam freely, and babies had shown precocious abilities to swim. However, these biological showcases were chased away from the town after being deemed dangerous, saving society from great upheaval.

The next spring, Margaret ran for re-election. The annual Delmar County Fair tried to attract a substitute judge. They couldn't find anyone. Instead they changed the rules and made it okay to buy your pie from a bakery. That fall, Evelyn's pie took first place again. She won every year until her death, in 2011, when an in-law baked the pie and took first prize too. Sometimes after judging, Margaret Lund would change the blue ribbon to purple to match her mood, and no one ever noticed.

Margaret Lund believed in honesty. But she also believed in second chances.

She bent toward Tyler. "Congratulations," she whispered. But once she was close she couldn't keep her mouth shut. "What was in your pie, Tyler?"

"I don't know what you're talking about, Mrs. Parrish."

"You said you didn't know if you could use store-bought crust, but I think you used the same one I bought Saturday. It was seventeen dollars."

"I didn't steal your crust," he said. The other kids in his group groaned. Tyler turned and waved them off and then shrank back, eyes down.

"Well, you did," Evelyn said, reaching for the ribbon. She stopped and stared at it for a long time. She would not cry, she told herself, not in front of everybody. "Thank you," she said loudly, and forced herself to say it again before walking out of the tent. Then she hurried to her car, climbing in awkwardly and slamming the door before letting her face fall.

Margot Hollister wasn't in line for the medals. She was at home, in bed with the flu. That night, when Evelyn got home, she sat down on the couch with the pie and lifted the cold plastic lid.

There were two servings left, with the tops crusted in red sugar crystals. Evelyn cut a generous wedge and burned her tongue on the first bite. Then she turned off the TV and put the pie box on the steps.

Tyler Nguyen. And my personal second place goes to Evelyn Parrish." Evelyn felt her stomach clench. Margaret never gave runner-up prizes.

On the way home Evelyn played Tyler's name over and over again in her head. She didn't know him, but she knew his family. Two years ago his mother had worked at the bake sale, selling Evelyn's rhubarb crumbles. She should have recognized the recipe. One of the things she'd done to make it her own was to sub in breadcrumbs for crackers—one of those little tips she had picked up from watching Walt's mother. Now Evelyn thought she could taste it in the crumble the way other people could taste the ingredients in a recipe. The breadcrumbs had given everything a depth, made the filling richer.

She hated herself for finding that interesting.

She fed piecrust to her parrot and ate biscoffs for dinner. Sooner or later Walt's mother was going to realize none of her fruit pies were being entered, and someone would call and ask if Evelyn was all right. And what would she say? Margaret rolled up the ribbon and offered it to Evelyn. Evelyn tried to say something. Margaret just looked at her, and Evelyn shook her head, tried to say thank you again.

Margaret's husband, Earl, nudged her with his elbow. "You don't have to say anything. She'll figure it out."

Margaret wasn't sure she'd done the right thing—not entirely. But baking pies together had been how Walter and Evelyn had met, and then again years later when their first marriage ended. Margaret was pretty sure Evelyn needed one last win more than Tyler did. Besides, Margaret thought, there were other ways to show Emma Nguyen that her son was special.

"Goddammit," Earl said as they left the tent. He and Margaret had been waiting all year for a chance to tell his niece how proud he was of her. The goddamn pie contest just got in the way.

Tyler opened his mouth. A few people started to clap.

"So that's how it is," he said. He wiped his hands on his jeans and spoke to Evelyn. "There aren't words," he said. He picked up the second-place ribbon, looked at it, and then back at Evelyn. "You didn't win," he said. "I did."

Margaret froze. She was holding her hands up as if to stop the clapping. "Let's save the speeches, folks," she said, and then, to Tyler, "What seems to be the problem?"

Tyler put his ribbon down on the table and looked at Evelyn. "I saw you," he said.

"I'm resigning," Margaret said. "I've had it."

Tyler was looking at Evelyn, but Margaret was looking at her, too.

"Don't hurt her." It came out sounding like a dare.

"I'm not going to hurt her," Margaret said.

"I mean it," Margaret said. "I'm leaving."

Tyler was a storm, but Margaret was pushing her hair back and looking a little queasy. The head of the Delmar County Fair was a broad man named Pete Warner. He had been working his way toward them, but when he saw Margaret was going to bolt, he changed direction and headed for Tyler.

Evelyn started to follow Margaret and realized she was instead following Tyler out into the open air behind the tent. Margaret was halfway down the row of food tents, but Evelyn was still behind Tyler.

"Stop her."

She heard the urgency in her own voice. Tyler turned, pink and stunned and still wet-faced. "I wish you would," he said, and then he was running.

Evelyn turned and ran. The tent flapped behind her. When she caught up to Margaret, Margaret was just starting to cry.

"I believe you," Evelyn said.

"I don't want to be there anymore," Margaret said, but then she was crying harder.

"I believe you," Evelyn said again.

Margaret was shorter than Evelyn but wider through the middle. And where Margaret could still stand up to take second place to Evelyn, she now had to turn sideways, and the two of them shrank down behind the high hedgerow that ran the back of the fairgrounds.

. . ." From then Evelyn didn't hear anything.

She thought she could hear Tyler saying something, but she wasn't sure. Then Evelyn saw the blue ribbon on her pie. Everyone was clapping. Margaret clapped, too. She picked up the second-place ribbon and pinned it to Tyler's pie. Tyler looked disappointed, then smiled. He held the pie out to Evelyn like he was giving her a present, and said, "You want to trade?"

But Evelyn said she didn't want to trade and took her pie home with her. For the first time in months she slept that night without dreaming about Walt. She woke before dawn with the crumbs that had fallen between her fingers still on the sheets, and for a minute couldn't breathe. But then she rolled out of bed, went into the kitchen, made coffee, and found the can of cherries right where she'd left it on the counter.

Margaret left the pie on the judging table and took the trophy over to Evelyn, then hugged her. The hug lasted a long time—long enough that Evelyn was almost starting to feel good about it, like some spark was lighting up inside her, when Margaret pulled back and said, "Give your husband a big hug for me."

Margaret had seen the box fall out of Evelyn's bag. But Evelyn hadn't slipped halfway out of her own life—at least not as much as Margaret had. But it was the divorce, five years ago, which had made Margaret what people in Harlow called unsympathetic. All Margaret's friends had daughters who'd left for college and husbands who'd left for someone else. They didn't talk much about how the loss felt or how lonely it was.

Margaret jingled her car keys as she and Evelyn walked out of the tent together. "You want a ride home?"

"Yes, thank you."

Margaret's driveway had a sag in it, and Margaret's mailbox leaned. Corn husks were weeded around the mums. Evelyn remembered this house: the last house, not counting foster homes. She must have been nine, maybe even eight, when her mother met the man who asked if she could come visit. The woman who answered the door looked just like Evelyn did now.

Inside, things were different. Margaret had mugs from cities Evelyn had never heard of. Evelyn had never known anyone, including her parents, who traveled. Snow globes sat on the mantlepiece: London Bridge, Manhattan, and the Sydney Opera House. The kitchen was painted yellow.

Evelyn realized Margaret was talking. "...Hollister's. I heard the owner say they could give you the discount because you put so much work into making it look homemade. I looked you up on Facebook."

Evelyn blinked.

"...I made pecan pie. I used to make an Army recipe I got out of a newspaper, but then they started adding all this stuff to butter, and I don't even know what 'partially hydrogenated palm fruit oil' is. I could just taste it was wrong."

Ursula K. Le Guin's classic story "The Ones Who Walk Away from Omelas" is the most reprinted SF story of all time (arguably for good reason). I read it for the first time in college and didn't like it, but I kept thinking about it in the years since, and in that way it was a perfect parable.

The main reason I didn't like it at the time was that I thought that all the suffering near Omelas was completely pointless. That wasn't quite true: there was a collective purpose, but the cost of maintaining it was too high for me. But the reason I kept thinking about it was because of the final line: "And they were not happy."

If you haven't read that story, you should. I might suggest you do so before continuing with the rest of this post.

My dislike of the cost-benefit tradeoff of Omelas never hit home, though, until this morning, when I was making pancakes for my daughter. A one-year-old has very little capacity for patience or delayed gratification, and my tradition of letting her stir the pancake batter by putting the immersion blender in her hand and standing clear wore out. She ran around with it while I tried to scrape pancake batter off the fridge and the chocolate pudding container. When I finally took it away and brought up my laptop to continue a proposal I'm writing, she flung it across the room. Glass shattered, sticky batter spattered across the counter, and the arm of the (classic) Oster blender whirligig landed near my wife's desk. My daughter wasn't concerned about any of that: she was immediately concerned about finding something else to spin around.

Moments later, after cleaning up the kitchen and anew count of the cost of parenting four-year-olds came into focus for me, I realized that the pain she caused was so minor compared to all she's brought to us that it was ridiculous for me to be upset. Then I felt guilty for feeling guilty; after all, she's only one, and it will all work out. That, I realized, is the pain in Omelas: necessary suffering for a collective good. Evelyn stepped forward, blinking a bit, and took the ribbon. Her hands were shaking so hard she nearly dropped it. She took the pie back to the car, sat inside on the passenger seat with it on her lap, and unclasped the box. The pie was fine. She opened it now and took out the note inside, something she'd written in a rush this morning, after she decided to take the pie from Hollister's and make it her own:

Dear Margaret,

Forgive me for my deception. The pie is as I said.

But the truth is, I hadn't baked anything since my husband died. I didn't know how to do it without him. Then I thought maybe if I just pretended, for a little while, I could remember how. Because that is the way it used to be: Walt carried the pies in, and I stood in back pretending not to care. And then he'd sneak up behind me, take my hands, and we'd laugh. That's all I really wanted back for a minute, the way things used to be.

I truly appreciate the ribbon. I hope you will understand.

Sincerely,
Evelyn Parrish

She laid the note on the wrapper beside her crumpled napkin. Then she took another forkful of pie and stared out the window as the sun went down. It would be dark soon. There was something sweet and sharp on her tongue, something like regret and something like honey.

"Are you sure? I tell people every year it's not a beauty contest. It's about the pie. And you both have pies that made me write 'Wow.' " She grinned at Tyler. "You got the crust just right, and the filling was perfect too. You're really something, you know? Some old guy in high school chemistry told me apples give off gases as they cook, and those gases make the crust get soggy if you don't let the apples cool first. I couldn't have told you that, but I could taste it." Tyler looked at his boots, smiling shyly.

Then Margaret turned back to Evelyn. "And your cherry. I know what I'm supposed to say about how the skin's supposed to stay shiny and not turn gray, but I can't even remember the last time I had a cherry pie that looked like that. But mine always taste like shoe leather. Yours, though, the filling was light as a feather, and the crust had that butterscotch snap I've been hunting for since I was twenty-nine and got married in a bowling alley." She winked. "Tell you what. Why don't you two split the ribbon and each of you take one of these little prizes home? It's a jar of Mrs. Siddons plum jam. Normally I don't give the runner-up anything, but in this case ..."

Margaret didn't seem surprised. "Well, which one did you bake, then?"

Her name had been called in a pie contest. Evelyn stood while the applause swelled and waved her arms a little, unsure whether to smile or not. Then she saw Margaret at the edge of the stage looking directly at her. This was not the tall, thin judge from registration this morning. Margaret was beaming. When the applause faded, Margaret called her over, and, so everyone could hear, said, "I can see why you'd be nervous to enter after all these years." She handed Evelyn the blue ribbon, pulling it through the little plastic clip at the top of the pie box. "But fifteen seconds out of my morning was worth eleven championships," she said.

Evelyn returned to her table and sat down. The pie still sat on the table, unmoved. No one seemed to have any idea who should cut it. Evelyn picked up the server, touched its edge to the surface of the crust, and then set it down again. Everyone stopped talking.

"All right," she said. "I guess I will."

She poured herself a slice, then dug the server back in and began to cut again. She had no appetite, but when you won a contest, people expected you to eat. She took a bite. It was sweet and tart and just loose enough and perfectly hot. It had been a very good pie.

As she chewed, she watched Tyler sitting alone at the corner of the next table. He wasn't looking at anyone. His shoulders were hunched and his face looked drawn, but then he caught her eye and half-smiled. So she offered him the rest of her slice, and when he shook his head, she cut another piece and set it on his plate. Then she nodded and went back to her own pie. No one was looking at her strangely now. The pie was delicious, the rest of it even better. And the world felt bigger than she'd remembered.

Evelyn sat at the kitchen table and ate the pie in small bites, the way Walt used to. She remembered the first year they'd entered together. Half of all her summers, when the peaches or cherries were in season. Half of every life she'd known.

What they don't tell you when you sign up to be a judge for anything, not at the county fair, not at the state spelling bee, not at the Boston Marathon, is that sooner or later you're going to get a test you can't pass. Sometimes it's a plate of dry cookies, and sometimes it's a seventeen-year-old girl who sets the standing high-jump record, and sometimes it's an old woman with a pie that looks like it came from a store.

You hope for a tie. There's always a quick and easy way to make a tie, and everyone walks away happy. But if you don't see one, you have to choose a winner, and then you step into a war zone.

Someone raised the tent wall and light streamed in. Evelyn stopped breathing until she realized no one was looking at her. Margaret wasn't, anyway. Margaret was smiling at Tyler. Tyler looked like a kicked puppy.

At the edge of the crowd, Evelyn waited for someone to come find her. But instead a woman with a baby carrier and a big, leafy basket of tomatoes stepped up. "Miss Parrish?" she said. "I'm Ellen Parker from the hardware store. I just had to tell you my sister swears by your rhubarb-strawberry and I've tried to make it myself, but the crust won't come out right. My husband keeps telling me I don't roll it out enough, but I think it's the butter. I wonder if you'd be willing to—"

Ellen went on. Margaret had moved on to the vegetable competition, and most of the crowd was making their way to the ice-cream social. After Ellen finished, a man carrying a salt-shaker-shaped pumpkin asked if she could suggest a way to keep his cornbread from falling apart. Someone else wanted the secret to her lemon meringue.

Evelyn looked at her pie, all lonely and perfect on the blue ribbon plate. She felt herself frowning, and then she looked at the people looking at her and she remembered the feeling of Walt standing by the back of the tent that first time, pretending not to care. She straightened her stature and sheigned in a warm, open way. 

When they'd all gone she gathered up the pie plates and walked them to the dish-return table. The teenage boy behind it asked if she was Evelyn Parrish. She nodded. He smiled and said, "My dad tried your recipe for sour cream chess pie, but he used honey instead of sugar and it didn't set right." 

"Oh," Evelyn said. 

"It's okay," the boy said. "Next time I'll try it the way you do."

Evelyn said, "Bring it to the fair and let me taste it, okay?" 

She drove home just as the sky turned lavender. In the kitchen, she turned on the overhead light and sat at the table. There was a sticky note on the fridge, written in Walt's large blocky handwriting the morning he died: Don't forget — contest is Friday. She stared at it for a long time.

—Evelyn Parrish." Margaret handed her the ribbon and paused as if waiting for something else to be said. Then she continued, "Usually I give the runner-up ribbon to the second best pie, but in this case I'd actually like to give a special mention to Tyler Nguyen. Some judges might not appreciate the subtle way in which you've managed to integrate the pineapple with the more traditional apple— It's very advanced. But it's also moving into a different category, and it wouldn't be fair to the people who worked really hard baking ordinary apple pies. I hope you'll enter next year in fruit combination." She paused again—long enough for a little smattering of relieved applause. Then smiled and turned back to Evelyn. "Congratulations." She handed Tyler a coupon for a dozen free cinnamon rolls, and then put her arms around Evelyn and hugged her. When they let go, Evelyn saw that Margaret was crying.

At the far end of the tent, Tyler Nguyen looked at his mother in disbelief. She shook her head at him and mouthed, You don't argue with the judge.

Tyler didn't argue. He folded his hands over the cinnamon-roll coupon and bowed his head like he was praying, but really he was trying not to grin. He was already planning his fruit combination pie for next year. A dragonfruit and starfruit medley with a creamsicle curd swirled in by hand, topped with aquafina foam and gold leaf. It would be beautiful. One taste and the whole county would know the difference between a combination and an integration. ♦

. . . Evelyn Parrish." The crowd clapped, and Margaret put the ribbon around the box.

Later, when all the judges and winners had posed for photos, Evelyn leaned over the table. "Would you please remove the lid? Just for a second? I want to see if I did the crimp right." Every pie at the fair was carefully exhibited under a glass dome, except for the winners, which were left in the open so people could take a closer look.

Margaret hesitated, but then she lifted off the dome and tapped it against the table. She slid the box toward Evelyn. Inside, the crust was lopsided. Two nickel-size spots at the edge had never risen at all.

"It's beautiful," Margaret said.

Evelyn tipped the pie toward her and smelled it, then touched the flat spots with her fingertip. "It doesn't look right," she said softly.

Margaret stared at the lopsided crust, then at Evelyn's hands. "The crust's not all that matters," she said. Beneath the table, Margaret took a small tin from her pocket and pressed something into Evelyn's palm.

Evelyn thought it was a mint at first, but then she recognized the waxy scent of butter. She raised her hand to her mouth, tasted it, and looked up at Margaret with tears in her eyes.

"Whisper about this all you want," Margaret said. "But don't you dare tell anyone I gave you the filling."

That was as far as she got before two thin girls in matching yellow T-shirts— Tyler's sisters, Evelyn thought angrily—yelled from the back of the tent. "Tyler!" The women at the table looked at each other, startled. Tyler Nguyen blushed and grinned and almost skipped to the front to accept the ribbon.

Margaret coughed and gestured grandly to Evelyn's pie. "And second place goes to Evelyn Parrish."

The tent erupted in applause, but no one clapped harder than Tyler Nguyen. His sisters squealed, he beamed at them, and they all hugged. After the awards were handed out, Tyler leaned across the table to Evelyn and said, "This is my first blue ribbon. Thanks for coming. It meant a lot. My mom's apples are kind of sour, so I used honey to make them sweet. In case you were wondering."

Evelyn nodded stiffly.

"That crust was perfect, too," he said. "I tried one of those French folds, but mine kind of sucked."

"It's a Dutch fold," she said automatically. Then she stopped herself, surprised at how much she wanted to talk to him about the pies, to explain that her crusts hadn't sucked at all this year. To tell him that last month, when she'd daringly pulled the ingredients for a Dutch apple out of the pantry, she'd had to add honey, too. But she just nodded again and forced a smile.

As she turned to leave, Tyler called after her, "Maybe we could do a bake-off sometime?" He sounded genuinely hopeful. Then his sisters tugged him away to take photos of the ribbon with their phone.

Evelyn stood for a moment, holding her pie, and stared at the place where Walt used to stand. A slow, warm ache uncoiled in her chest, almost a smile. She looked at the pie in her hands and realized she didn't hate it after all. She decided to walk home so she could eat it outside and watch the sun go down over the corn.

...Evelyn Parrish. But I want to say a few words about the runner-up. Tyler Nguyen's apple pie was just as good as Evelyn's—there's no shame in that—it's just that Evelyn's was good in a completely different way, and that's what we're looking for in a true baking competition."

She pinned the blue ribbon on Evelyn's pie, handed the red one to Tyler, and turned to Evelyn, who was staring at the table. "There's a lesson here for all of us," Margaret said, holding the pie up so everyone could see the perfect edge with the crimping on the bottom as well as the top. "And I'm not talking about the crimp. I'm talking about how someone who hasn't made a single pie in four months—and who, let's be honest, hadn't won a contest in years anyway—how they came back and took first place just by listening."

Margaret put her arm around Evelyn's shoulders and squeezed. "Congratulations, Evelyn. And welcome back."

At that moment Evelyn realized that she hadn't missed making pies after all. She had just missed entering them. But now that she was back, maybe it was time to stop looking over her shoulder and start thinking about what she would make next year. Something that didn't exist yet.

She took her pie back to the car, careful not to jostle the box. When she got home she tucked the blue ribbon under the salt shaker on the kitchen windowsill, then opened the freezer, pulled out the box of frozen raspberries she'd bought that morning, and got started on the first blackberry-raspberry sour cream pie Harlow might ever see.

Everyone clapped, including Tyler, who looked surprised and delighted. He took a bow. But Evelyn wasn't clapping. Margaret wasn't looking at her. The girl next to her elbows her and grins. Evelyn keeps her hands folded in her lap and refuses to clap.

Afterward Tyler and his mother smile and thank everyone, and Margaret clears the table and puts the ribbons away. But she doesn't leave. She walks to where Evelyn is sitting and she sits beside her and says, "I'm sorry about Walt."

Evelyn nods, but doesn't say anything. Margaret pats her hand. "You must miss him an awful lot."

"I do," Evelyn says. And then, unable to stop herself, she says, "But I wouldn't have cheated." She takes the ribbon out of her pocket and hands it to Margaret. "Give it to him."

Margaret looks at her. She shakes her head and stands up. "You baked it, didn't you?"

"As much as he did. I bought the pie, but I crimped the edge and I made the lattice top and I let it cool on my countertop," Evelyn says. "It was a Parrish pie."

Margaret stares at her for a moment and then bursts out laughing. Evelyn joins her. They laugh together, and then Margaret hugs Evelyn, and Evelyn cries. "Enter next year," Margaret says when they both have stopped.

"I might," Evelyn says.

People clapped. Tyler looked surprised but seemed pleased anyway. He'd just moved here from California; Evelyn had brought him an extra slice of gingerbread when he'd been homesick at Christmas. Before she could see Tyler again, Evelyn was ushered outside by the fair manager to take photos with the ribbon wrapped around the pie box. She held the pie up for the camera and tried to smile, but it felt like something heavy was pressing on her chest.

She didn't taste the pie until the next morning. At first she didn't recognize the flavor—cherry, yes, but underneath it something intricate and nutty, something that made the pastry taste richer and the filling brighter. She ate a second slice, then a third, standing at the counter with the pie in one hand and the ingredients list in the other. All the ingredients were the same ones she'd usually used. It took her a moment to realize what had happened. Somehow, just for this once, she'd meant the pie.

In the weeks that followed, people at church and the grocery store asked Evelyn if she'd entered the county fair again next year. She found herself saying yes before she had a chance to think.

Then last night she'd had a dream. She was standing at the back of the tent as her husband Walt brought out her pie. He was wearing his old brown strut shoes, the ones with the tassels. But when he lifted the cloth off the pie, she saw that the crust was crimped, the way she never quite got it, not with her swollen arthritis fingers, not the way she'd seen Walt do it fifteen or twenty years ago. Tyler Nguyen was standing beside her in the dream, holding his apple pie, and the two of them were smiling at each other like old friends, like people who understood each other without having to say a word. Evelyn chuckled, picturing that, and pulled the ribbon through the handle of her tote bag. "Thank you, Margaret," she said.

They watched a curious crow hop across the asphalt together, side-stepping its own shadow.

Why had she made the pie?

She made the pie because everyone at church kept asking if she was entering the contest this year, and she couldn't face explaining to them that she wasn't going to bake a pie after her husband's death.

This was not a true victory for Evelyn in the sense that she hadn’t actually baked the pie herself, which was against the contest’s rules. She used a store-bought pie and only redid the crust, but she didn’t bake it. Winning under these circumstances felt like a hollow achievement because it wasn’t accomplished through her own genuine effort, especially following her husband's death, which had made baking difficult for her emotionally.

But I also knew she was distracted, unwell, and she is, after all, eleven-time champion. That meant something once, and I see no reason it shouldn't mean something now."

Evelyn didn't go to the supermarket that week. She got her groceries delivered, and Ben Hamm left two organic honeycrisps on her porch with a note that read "For baking." She waited until the first cold night and left the house at seven o'clock, driving with her headlights off so no one would see her until the beams came on by themselves. When she arrived at the fairgrounds, the tent was empty except for Margaret Lund, who was stacking chairs.

"I wasn't trying to trick you," Evelyn said.

"I know," Margaret said. The sweep of her arm took in the silent, dark grandstands. "People bake for all sorts of reasons. I'd say the only ones we need to worry about are the ones who aren't trying at all." She handed Evelyn a blue ribbon still wrapped in cellophane. "Would you hang onto this for me?"

"Your first place?"

"Technically, yes." Margaret smiled in the half-light. "But don't let that go to your head. It was a very close year."

"What did you write on your clipboard before you gave me the ribbon?"

Margaret Lund looked at her for a moment. Then she reached into the pocket of her blazer and pulled out a small blue notebook.

"See for yourself," she said.

Margaret Lund was a fair and honest judge. She prided herself on being impartial. But she also knew everyone's children in Harlow and Delmar. She recognized Evelyn's fancy crimp from the distance. She understood how it felt to miss someone who was gone. And she believed everyone deserved a little happiness.

"Tyler, thank you so much for your excellent pie," Margaret announced. "And congratulations to Evelyn Parrish, who takes home this year's blue ribbon."

Evelyn blinked as the crowd started to clap. Tyler stood frozen for a moment, then smiled and held up his pie in a little salute.

Later a few people stopped Evelyn to admire her pie. She tried to be pleasant. But every time she glanced at Tyler, who was glumly dismantling his own crust in the parking lot, her victory felt hollow. On the drive home, Evelyn made up her mind: next year, she would bake her own pie, or not enter at all.

Evelyn pushed back her empty chair, picked up her tote bag, and walked out of the fairground's barbed-wire fence. "Who's going to get into a piece of pie at four o'clock in the afternoon? Be the death of me," said Walt. She heard him laughing.

Evelyn unlocked her car and opened the trunk, pushing her tote bag in along with her purse and her black lace umbrella. She slid into the driver's seat, turned on the ignition, and let the engine idle for a minute before starting down the gravel road. She passed the empty fairgrounds, made a left at the stop sign, and accelerated on the highway toward home.

Evelyn had been driving for almost a mile when a cloud of dust puffed out of the dry grass by the side of the road. "What now?" she said out loud.

The dust chased after her, closing the gap between them. It slowed to a trot and then to a walk. It stood, shivering slightly with the heat of the day.

Evelyn pressed the brake pedal, then lifted her foot off. The dust was still there. She tapped her brakes again and it became a shadow-a long one. She stopped, putting the car in park. The shadow moved forward.

Evelyn looked in her mirror. "Go away," she said. She rolled up the windows, unlocked the car doors, and put her key in the cup holder. Then she opened the driver's door.

The shadow moved on, walking across the highway toward the old gas station. Evelyn turned on her hazard lights and ran after it, bare feet slapping on the highway. By the time she reached the station, it had disappeared inside.

Evelyn leaned on the porch rail, closed her eyes, and took a deep breath.

2 cups de-seeded cherries cut in half

1/2 cup sugar

1/4 teaspoon salt

1 tablespoon cornstarch

1/2 teaspoon lemon extract

Gently heat cherries with 1/4 cup water to cooking temperature. Cook, stirring occasionally, for 17 minutes. While cherries are heating, mix remaining ingredients. Add to cherries.
